articles.title: Panama is one battle in China’s infrastructure war
articles.summary: China has retaliated against Panama by increasing inspections and detentions of Panamanian-flagged ships after the Panamanian Supreme Court struck down concessions held by a Hong Kong-based company at the entrance terminals of the Panama Canal.
articles.body:
Panama is paying a price for stepping away from Beijing. Recent reporting indicates that Chinese authorities have sharply increased inspections and detentions of Panamanian-flagged ships after Panama’s Supreme Court struck down the concessions held by Hong Kong-based CK Hutchison at the Balboa and Cristobal container terminals. Beijing says the measures are based on safety concerns. Panamanian officials see them as retaliation for a decision that weakened China’s commercial position at both ends of the Panama Canal.

Panama is one battle in a much larger contest over who will shape the Western Hemisphere. For more than two decades, China expanded its reach by financing, building, and operating ports, railways, electrical grids, telecommunications systems, logistics hubs, and energy projects across Latin America. Those investments created influence that extends well beyond commerce.

But Washington has begun pushing back. The dispute in Panama offers an early look at how difficult it may be to reverse two decades of Chinese infrastructure expansion.

My first assignment after joining the U.S. Army was in the Panama Canal Zone. While serving there, I came to appreciate the canal as much more than a waterway connecting the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. It remains one of the greatest engineering achievements in history and a lasting reminder of what American vision, resources and determination can accomplish.

Built under the direction of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers after overcoming disease, unforgiving terrain and immense technical challenges, the canal transformed global commerce while giving the United States an enduring strategic advantage in the Western Hemisphere.

One of us recently returned from Panama, where conversations repeatedly turned to China’s presence around the canal and across the country. Many Americans have only recently begun paying attention. Panamanians have watched this expansion unfold for years. The U.S. allowed its attention to drift while Chinese companies steadily pursued projects near one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints, less than four hours by air from Miami.

Panama recognized the People’s Republic of China in 2017 , ended diplomatic relations with Taiwan, and joined the Belt and Road Initiative the following year. Chinese firms pursued the proposed Panama City-David railway, the Fourth Bridge over the Panama Canal, the Amador Cruise Terminal, and other large projects.

The greatest concern centered on the Balboa and Cristobal terminals at the Pacific and Atlantic entrances to the canal, operated by Panama Ports Company, a subsidiary of CK Hutchison. China did not own or operate the canal, but companies tied to Beijing had gained influence over commercial infrastructure surrounding it.

Panama is not unique. China’s state-owned COSCO Shipping built and now operates the deep-water port at Chancay in Peru. State Grid of China invested heavily in Brazil’s electricity transmission network. Chinese firms expanded into energy, mining, transportation and telecommunications throughout the region. In Venezuela, more than $60 billion in Chinese lending helped secure access to oil while China supported the Maduro regime through years of isolation.

Each deal had its own commercial explanation, yet the larger result was a network of Chinese influence spread across ports, power systems, supply chains and national economies.

Washington increasingly viewed Chinese influence surrounding the canal as a national security concern. It elevated the issue in discussions with Panama, encouraged greater American investment, and supported efforts that led CK Hutchison to agree to sell its controlling interest in the terminals to a U.S.-led consortium.

Panama also withdrew from China’s Belt and Road Initiative . When Chinese opposition delayed the proposed sale, Panama’s Supreme Court struck down the port concessions, clearing the way for new management. Panama became the first visible effort to reverse a much broader Chinese strategy built on infrastructure throughout Latin America.

Beijing’s response illustrates why control of infrastructure matters. Ports move trade, electrical grids power economies, telecommunications systems carry information, and logistics hubs connect global supply chains. Once countries become dependent on those systems, commercial relationships can become political leverage. Panama’s shipping registry is now feeling that pressure through delays, inspections, and the possibility that shipowners will move their vessels elsewhere.

Panama will not be the last contest over Chinese infrastructure in the Western Hemisphere. Similar battles are likely wherever ports, railroads, electrical grids, telecommunications networks and logistics hubs intersect with national security.

China spent more than two decades building this position through investment, construction and long-term commercial relationships rather than military force. Reversing it will require the U.S. to compete with the same patience and persistence that allowed Beijing to build it in the first place.

John Spencer is the chair of war studies at the Madison Policy Forum, where Frank Viola is a fellow.

images.caption: FILE – A Panama Canal worker docks the Chinese container ship Cosco at the Panama Canals’ Cocoli Locks, in Panama City on Dec. 3, 2018. China’s Belt and Road initiative has built power plants, roads, railroads and ports around the world and deepened China’s relations with Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Mideast. It is a major part of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s push for China to play a larger role in global affairs. (AP Photo/Arnulfo Franco, File)

articles.title: Trump shows off White House construction projects: ‘We get the best stuff’
articles.summary: President Trump on Wednesday showed reporters a closer look at the White House’s various construction projects, including the ballroom and new helipad, saying “we get the best stuff.” Trump led an uninterrupted, 30-minute tour of the new White House helipad designed for Marine One, which, when completed, will be 100 feet wide, made of granite…
articles.body:
President Trump on Wednesday showed reporters a closer look at the White House’s various construction projects, including the ballroom and new helipad , saying “we get the best stuff.”

Trump led an uninterrupted, 30-minute tour of the new White House helipad designed for Marine One, which, when completed, will be 100 feet wide, made of granite and adorned with the presidential seal. Trump signed the underside of the slab while talking to reporters.

The president also praised the slab’s durability and said it will be “here for a long time.”

“We get the best stuff; one thing I know how to do is build,” he told reporters .

Trump heralded how the helipad will “look incredible from the air and from every place else” and highlighted that it will be used for celebratory events and meetings, including his upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Workers told the president that the landing pad will be completed by Sept. 21, two days before Xi’s planned arrival.

“We might make it for President Xi,” Trump replied. “That’d be nice but not imperative.”

The granite used for the helipad measures at 4 inches thick and was dug out of a quarry in California, with “The Seal of the United States of America” carved into it, Reuters reported .

“This will be much better for state arrivals,” the president ​said. “And in fact, instead of being on grass, now they’ll be using that almost like a table. They can have events on it. They can have ​people go there for cocktails and then walk to the ballroom after that’s finished.”

He also emphasized the durability of the slab, saying it will “be here long after we’re gone, no matter what happens with the world, this is not moving. This will take any kind of shot.”

He requested earlier this month that construction crews tear up the helipad after he was frustrated with its appearance, according to The Washington Post . Two people familiar with the project told the outlet that the president had expressed interest in adding a landing pad level with the horizon, which would require disassembling the helipad and leveling the South Lawn.

“Nice job, fellas. Does anybody know the word ‘media’? This is serious media and you guys are doing a great job. Sorry to take an extra week and a half, but lifting it up was one of the best things we’ve ever done,” Trump told crews working on the helipad on Wednesday, confirming the Post’s reporting.

He celebrated the driveway leading up to the southern portico, as well, saying there were previously potholes in the roadway.

“It’s ridiculous the way this place was taken care of,” Trump continued. “Nobody, including other presidents, they didn’t see it. But I see it because I was very good at real estate, like maybe the best, in a lot of ways. I love construction. I love seeing things properly taken care of.”

The president also took notice of the two flagpoles on the northern and southern sides of the White House, which he donated to himself.

“This is a great pole,” Trump said. “This is a top-of-the-line — it’s tapered. This isn’t a straight up-and-down job, which looks terrible, frankly. It’s a tapered pole, great — I’m very good at flagpoles.”

The walls of the White House ballroom towered behind everyone as construction on the planned 90,000-square-foot addition to the executive mansion went on.

“We’ve gotten tremendous architectural reviews,” he said about the project. “It’s beautiful.”

The National Trust for Historic Preservation is challenging the project, arguing to the Supreme Court on Tuesday that the administration’s emergency request to allow construction must be denied. The Trump administration wants the justices to step in to stop a lower court order that would grind the above-ground work to a halt starting at the end of the day on Friday.

Trump characterized his effort to revamp the White House as long overdue

“This building was falling apart,” he told reporters. “It’s falling apart –– like buying a building in New York City that’s in bad shape ​and putting it back together. That’s what I used to do. I did it better than anybody, I think.”

images.caption: President Trump speaks outside the White House, Aug. 19, 2026, in Washington, at the construction site of the new helicopter landing zone on the South Lawn of the White House.

articles.title: Reform UK proposes tax rebates for firms to boost apprenticeships
articles.summary: Suella Braverman also advised student's "not to get ripped off by the great university scam".
articles.body:
Young apprentices should have part of their wages paid by taxpayers, according to Reform UK plans , external aimed at delivering a "skills revolution".

The party's education spokeswoman Suella Braverman said a Reform government would introduce an "apprenticeship wage credit" offering small and medium-sized businesses a 30% rebate on the wages of apprentices they take on aged 16 to 18.

She also advised students receiving their GCSE exam results on Thursday "not to get ripped off by the great university scam" and to learn a trade instead.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he wants teenagers to have technical routes into careers that could rival the path of a traditional university degree.

The government has been introducing changes and examining ways to encourage more young people into work, including giving some parents on benefits up to £4,500 a year to encourage their children to start apprenticeships.

Former minister Alan Milburn has been tasked with investigating why so many young people are not in employment, education or training - known by the acronym Neets.

Reform said its announcement was the first in a series of proposals aimed at reaching 600,000 apprenticeship starts per year by the end of the next Parliament, likely to be 2034.

The party says it would pay for its plans by banning all foreign students from accessing taxpayer-funded loans and stopping what the party calls "Mickey Mouse degrees".

Reform said its policy, which also includes a £2,000 retention bonus for apprentices, could cost between £1.48bn and almost £2bn over five years.

Braverman said there are "excessive number of graduates with qualifications that don't match the skills needed for our country," arguing that learning a trade would be a better use of their time.

Apprentices are generally paid a lower wage but get on-the-job training and practical work experience.

Speaking at a press conference, Braverman said: "We're firing the starting gun on unleashing a technical and vocational renaissance of homegrown skills.

"Reform will not do this because it fills us with some jingoistic pride but because we will do what it takes to save Britain from the perpetual doom loop of decline, debt and despair that we're currently in."

The MP said the apprenticeship wage credit would result in businesses saving an average of £4,000-a-year per apprentice.

The £2,000 tax-free retention bonus would be paid to workers who "show loyalty" by staying with the business that trained them for at least two years after they complete their apprenticeship, said Braverman.

Asked if the policy would mean some universities would have to close, Braverman said she did not envisage that but instead suggested universities need to "repurpose" themselves into construction colleges and manufacturing colleges.

When pressed to give examples of "Mickey Mouse degrees", Braverman pointed to "gender studies" and "golf course studies".

She said: "There's not a necessity, there's not a value in many of these degrees."

The British and International Golf Greenkeepers Association (BIGGA) has previously criticised Braverman for similar remarks, which they branded "negligent and potentially damaging".

BIGGA chief executive Jim Croxton said: "Golf course management is a growing industry with currently more vacancies than qualified applicants.

"Anyone successfully studying for a degree in this field is effectively guaranteed employment in a vibrant industry."

A Labour Party spokesperson said all young people "deserve a clear route to a good career" whether through "a properly funded apprenticeship, high-quality technical education or university".

The spokesperson added: "That's exactly what this Labour government is already delivering, with 500,000 new jobs, apprenticeships and training opportunities to help young people earn or learn, including a guaranteed job for 18–24-year-olds who have been out of work for 18 months."

On Wednesday, Conservative shadow education secretary Laura Trott said there is demand for apprenticeships but claimed the Labour government "aren't doing enough to boost supply".

She said: "Our New Deal for Young People would axe the dead end degrees that don't lead to jobs and instead invest in apprenticeships giving school leavers more choice."

Liberal Democrat universities spokesperson Ian Sollom said it was important to protect local colleges and universities as well as boosting apprenticeships, including apprenticeships in degree courses.

"Reform's proposals amount to dangerous economic vandalism which would rip a multi-billion-pound hole in our world-leading university sector," he added.

Green Party MP Hannah Spencer, who was a plumber before becoming an MP, said: "People are tired of Reform pitting us against each other - Those of us that did apprenticeships can still see the value in degrees and everyone should be able to choose their own path of education."

She added the Greens had announced a windfall tax on big banks , which she said would support small businesses employing more young people.

images.caption: Image caption, Suella Braverman takes part in a painting and decorating lesson with apprentices at McLoughlin Group Holdings, in Enfield, north London

articles.title: Alina Habba says she’s ‘not in the running’ to replace Leavitt
articles.summary: Alina Habba, the president’s former personal attorney, ruled herself out as a candidate for White House press secretary as speculation swirls about whom President Trump will pick to replace Karoline Leavitt. “Flattered by the Kalshi odds, but I’m not in the running for any job,” Habba wrote in a social media post on Wednesday, referring…
articles.body:
Alina Habba, the president’s former personal attorney, ruled herself out as a candidate for White House press secretary as speculation swirls about whom President Trump will pick to replace Karoline Leavitt.

“Flattered by the Kalshi odds, but I’m not in the running for any job,” Habba wrote in a social media post on Wednesday, referring to the popular prediction market. “However, if I’m getting a new one, I’d love for one of these anonymous sources to let me know first.”

Habba is one of several public figures and people close to the president who are believed to be on a shortlist of potential candidates to replace Leavitt, who is slated to leave the White House this month.

Leavitt, the only person to serve as Trump’s press secretary during his second term, announced earlier this month she was leaving the job to spend more time with her family.

The top spokesperson for Trump’s 2024 campaign, she recently had a second child.

Habba made a name for herself in the media defending Trump while he was out of office and faced various charges relating to his businesses, handling of classified documents and attempts to overturn the 2020 election.

“Fake news remains the undefeated champ,” Habba wrote in her social media post. “Well…until I come at them.”

articles.title: Trump can reduce hostility for immigration enforcement — without weakening it
articles.summary: There are changes Trump can make in enforcing his immigration to reduce hostilities and the number of legal challenges.
articles.body:
Border czar Tom Homan has had record-breaking success with his border security measures. Apprehensions at the Southwest border have declined to levels not seen in more than three decades. This is because, as the Department of Homeland Security claims, the border is more secure now than at any point in history .

The Trump administration has had success with interior enforcement, too, but its enforcement measures there have resulted in a lot of public hostility and a tsunami of lawsuits. But it doesn’t have to be this way. President Trump can implement his enforcement policies just as effectively, but with less hostility and fewer lawsuits, if he just adopts a few smart changes.

First, his administration should change its litigation strategy. The ACLU brought 434 legal actions against Trump during his first term in office, and 230 legal actions against him during just the first year of his second term. The best way to stop or weaken this campaign to block Trump’s immigration policies is to learn as much as possible about what the activist organization is doing and why.

A January ACLU report titled “ Defeat, Delay, Dilute: ACLU Versus President Trump ” explains the strategy. The administration also should study the ACLU’s successful lawsuits to learn how to make new enforcement initiatives less vulnerable to avoidable litigation.

A second tip pertains to the use of masks and badges. Homan says that ICE officers in the field need masks to protect them and their families from what has been called doxxing, or the malicious exposure of their personal information. It is a crime to make personal information about ICE officers available to the public, to to threaten or incite violence against officers and their families, who are just doing their jobs.

The strongest objection to face masks is that they reduce accountability. This is a legitimate concern, but ICE officers can be identified even if they are wearing masks. The agency can assign unique identification numbers to each officer and put those numbers and the names of the offices they work for on badges. Then simply require them to wear the badges when they are conducting field operations. This would substantially reduce the risk of doxxing, while the identities of the numbered officers could be made available to the ICE Office of Professional Responsibility , the Homeland Security inspector general , and congressional oversight committees as needed.

Third, the Executive Office for Immigration Review is using military lawyers as temporary immigration judges without requiring them to have direct immigration experience. This is intended to address a growing backlog of cases at the courts. But using judges inexperienced in immigration law unnecessarily increases the risk of reversible error and due process challenges. It would be better to use these lawyers primarily to preside over master calendar hearings until they have more experience.

As the office puts it, “Master calendar hearings are held for pleadings, scheduling, and other similar matters. It should be possible to train these newcomers for these responsibilities and to handle relatively straightforward in-absentia proceedings for aliens who fail to appear at the master calendar hearings despite receiving proper notification. This way, more experienced immigration judges can handle more complex matters.

ICE should also reexamine its priorities for detention. As of July 11, ICE was detaining 65,765 immigrants, but many of these might not need to be detained. The agency should give priority to detaining aliens who are subject to mandatory detention , which includes the 90-day “ removal period ” for aliens with a final removal order. When detention is discretionary, ICE generally should release aliens unless an individual assessment indicates that detention is necessary due to a public safety or flight risk. In questionable cases, ICE’s Alternatives to Detention program can be used to minimize the risk that aliens will abscond.

In May, the Department of Homeland Security shut down the Office of the Immigration Detention Ombudsman that provided independent oversight of immigration detention facilities because Congress had not provided funding for that office. Its responsibilities included handling complaints about conditions in detention facilities.

The department should ask Congress to restore funding for this office. In addition to helping immigrants subject to detention, it provides an independent mechanism for identifying and correcting problems before they become scandals or lawsuits.

According to a recent Economist-YouGov poll , 48 percent of Americans support abolishing ICE, and 40 percent oppose abolishing it. Moreover, 42 percent do not have any confidence in ICE, 11 percent have only a little, and only 22 percent have a great deal of confidence in the agency. Fifty-eight percent think ICE has used too much force; only 30 percent think its use of force has been necessary and justified.

ICE’s Office of Public Affairs is supposed to prevent such negative reactions to enforcement operations. It should redouble its efforts to bolster public confidence.

Better-trained judges, unique numbers for identifying masked officers without exposing them, the elimination of unnecessary detentions, the restoration of an independent detention-complaint office and greater transparency would all make enforcement measures more defensible legally and politically, without reducing their effectiveness.

Nolan Rappaport was detailed to the House Judiciary Committee as an executive branch immigration law expert for three years. He subsequently served as an immigration counsel for the Subcommittee on Immigration, Border Security and Claims for four years. Prior to working on the Judiciary Committee, he wrote decisions for the Board of Immigration Appeals for 20 years.

articles.title: Scavino warns officials fired for doing ‘s‑‑‑ty job’ against media attacks
articles.summary: White House deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino tore into unnamed former staffers in a profanity-laced post on social media, telling those who had been fired or passed over for jobs to stop bashing the administration in the media and “take the L.” “When you get fired for doing a spectacularly s—ty job at an…
articles.body:
White House deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino tore into unnamed former staffers in a profanity-laced post on social media, telling those who had been fired or passed over for jobs to stop bashing the administration in the media and “take the L.”

“When you get fired for doing a spectacularly s—ty job at an agency, with your badge deactivated, building access revoked, and the full ‘you’re dead to us’ package — or when you get passed over for Ambassadorships, Boards, or Commissions — because there are candidates who are actually far more qualified than you, please resist the urge to sprint to every media outlet that will platform your lying bull s—, and then falsely attack the people in the Presidential Personnel Office who are out here serving President Trump, the Administration, and the American people each and every day,” Scavino wrote on the social platform X .

“Just take the L, and move on, LOSER,” he added.

Scavino, one of President Trump’s longest-serving aides, did not say whom the late Wednesday post was directed toward, though several prominent figures have been fired or left their posts throughout Trump’s second term.

FBI Director Kash Patel backed the rant , writing from his personal X account, “Boss Move, Dan’s a legend.”

Several Trump allies also pondered whom the aide may have been referencing in his post.

Far-right influencer and Trump loyalist Laura Loomer wrote on X : “Wonder who he is talking about.” White House principal deputy communications director Kaelan Dorr also threw his support behind the rant in a series of emojis .

Scavino has led the Presidential Personnel Office since last year while continuing to serve as White House deputy chief of staff. His office oversees the selection and vetting of thousands of political appointees across the federal government.

His critique comes as tensions over potential leaks and public criticisms from inside Trump’s orbit have spilled into the media in recent weeks. The White House has also brushed off waves of scrutiny surrounding the close relationship between Trump and his executive assistant Natalie Harp.

articles.title: O’Reilly: Trump endorsement ‘doesn’t have the cachet that it did’ because of Iran
articles.summary: Political commentator Bill O’Reilly on Wednesday said an endorsement from President Trump “doesn’t have the cachet that it did” previously, citing the Iran war. O’Reilly and NewsNation’s Chris Cuomo talked about Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.), who secured the Republican nomination in Florida’s gubernatorial race. Trump has endorsed Donalds, but the candidate said it is the…
articles.body:
Political commentator Bill O’Reilly on Wednesday said an endorsement from President Trump “doesn’t have the cachet that it did” previously, citing the Iran war.

O’Reilly and NewsNation’s Chris Cuomo talked about Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.), who secured the Republican nomination in Florida’s gubernatorial race. Trump has endorsed Donalds, but the candidate said it is the president’s decision regarding whether to hit the campaign trail with the Florida lawmaker.

“I don’t know if that means anything now, because Donald Trump has got to solve the Iran thing,” O’Reilly said during his “Cuomo” appearance. “That is really hurting him. Because then the prices follow that. They’re haunting him. So I don’t know if the endorsement –– it’s not going to hurt you if you’re a Republican. No, but it doesn’t have the cachet that it did.”

O’Reilly predicted that Donalds will win the November election and succeed Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R), “but it’ll be close” unless Donalds can “shake” Florida Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly in a debate.

Cuomo then pressed the former Fox News host on Trump’s handling of the Iran war, its impact on the economy and its unpopularity among Americans, and if Trump can “save your party from having to own your mistake?”

“Listen, I don’t get the daily briefings,” O’Reilly replied. “I don’t know what the intel is. All I know is that this is tied into President Trump’s legacy now. This is personal, as they said in ‘The Godfather’: ‘It’s business, not personal, Sonny,’ OK? So he’s got to come out as the winner in Iran somehow.”

O’Reilly said there is “no doubt” Trump will not sell taking over Iran’s Kharg Island, which holds around 90 percent of Iran’s crude oil exports. Cuomo said that selling the war “is the big problem he has.”

O’Reilly said he was “not sure about that,” emphasizing the Trump administration’s claim that preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon prompted the conflict.

Republican lawmakers have largely stood behind Trump in his military action against Iran, but some have expressed that it could be a political liability come November. Democrats have used the conflict as part of their messaging on the campaign trail.

Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.), whose term ends in January, recently warned that the Iran conflict could be the U.S.’s “ next forever war .”

“And I think it is with gas prices rising again and our oil reserves going down, this is, you know, problematic for a lot of reasons because … the Iran conflict is not on the ballot in November, but affordability is, and the cost of living is, and this thing has increased our cost of living,” she said.

The Iran war could also depress Republican turnout ahead of the midterms, according to polling taken by Politico in July.

Retiring Rep. Michael McCaul (R-Texas) told CNN at the time that the U.S. should negotiate “from the rubble.”

“I think this back-and-forth approach is not the right one, and it will guarantee that this thing delays into the midterm elections, which is precisely what Iran is trying to do right now,” he said.

articles.title: Ocasio-Cortez backs Markey in Massachusetts Senate primary
articles.summary: Democratic Sen. Ed Markey (Mass.) received a boost to his reelection bid Thursday with an endorsement from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.). Markey is engaged in a competitive Democratic primary race against Rep. Seth Moulton (D-Mass.). The two candidates have sought to build upon a growing antiestablishment sentiment in the Democratic Party in their campaigns. Moulton…
articles.body:
Democratic Sen. Ed Markey (Mass.) received a boost to his reelection bid Thursday with an endorsement from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.).

Markey is engaged in a competitive Democratic primary race against Rep. Seth Moulton (D-Mass.). The two candidates have sought to build upon a growing antiestablishment sentiment in the Democratic Party in their campaigns.

Moulton has said it is time for generational change in his bid to replace the 80-year-old incumbent senator, while Markey has argued his “experience is not the opposite of change.”

Ocasio-Cortez lauded Markey’s legislative record on issues like affordability and clean energy, citing their work together on the Green New Deal in Congress.

“At a time when powerful special interests are making life harder for everyday Americans, Massachusetts working families need a champion in the U.S. Senate to stand up for them and fight corporate greed,” Ocasio-Cortez said in a statement .

“Ed Markey has spent his career doing exactly that, from our partnership on the Green New Deal to running his campaign without accepting a dime of corporate PAC money,” she continued. “His work is an inspiration to many of us who are committed to building a better future for all, and that’s why I’m proud to endorse him.”

Markey and Moulton will face off in a final debate Thursday evening ahead of the primary election on Sept. 1.

The incumbent senator thanked Ocasio-Cortez for her support in a statement Thursday morning. Markey is also backed by progressives like Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Elizabeth Warren (Mass.).

“We introduced the Green New Deal to tackle the climate crisis, lower costs, and build an economy that works for working people, not corporations and billionaires,” Markey said. “I am incredibly proud to have her endorsement and look forward to continuing to fight alongside her for the livable future we deserve.”

Moulton has garnered support from Democrats like New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill and Reps. Derek Tran (Calif.), Chrissy Houlahan (Pa.), Seth Magaziner (R.I.) and Pat Ryan (N.Y.).

articles.title: Exclusive: US says ‘significant deterioration’ in China’s treatment of detained American academic
articles.summary: Chinese authorities are increasing restrictions on a wrongfully detained American academic, prompting U.S. officials to express alarm about a “significant deterioration” in his treatment, according to sources familiar with the matter. Min Zin, an American citizen who runs a think tank focused on politics in Myanmar, was arrested in China in June. The Trump administration…
articles.body:
Chinese authorities are increasing restrictions on a wrongfully detained American academic, prompting U.S. officials to express alarm about a “significant deterioration” in his treatment, according to sources familiar with the matter.

Min Zin, an American citizen who runs a think tank focused on politics in Myanmar, was arrested in China in June . The Trump administration on Thursday designated him as “wrongfully detained,” a powerful label that makes advocating for his release a top U.S. priority.

The timing of this action is significant. President Trump is expected to welcome Chinese President Xi Jinping for a state visit on Sept. 24.

Advocates say Trump does have an impressive record of freeing Americans jailed abroad — estimated at more than 100 individuals — and non-Americans, to include political prisoners, individuals kidnapped by terrorist organizations and those persecuted for their religion.

Min Zin’s family and friends hope the designation adds increased urgency for his release, raising concern that his detention is at an unknown location, blocking U.S. consular officials from observing his living conditions. They are only able to meet him at a hotel when he is made available by Chinese authorities. During the last visit, Chinese authorities placed Min Zin at the far end of a conference table, making communication difficult and having a chilling effect on the conversation.

Min Zin’s wife, Sylvia Zin, thanked Trump for formally designating her husband as wrongfully detained, and she described the heartache felt from his absence for more than two months — missing a family vacation, his 14-year-old daughter’s first day of high school and her performing in a school concert. She also said the family will likely be apart for Min Zin’s birthday on Sept. 9.

“This will be the first time in her life that our family is broken apart for a birthday,” she said.

Min Zin, who had a 10-year visa to enter China and was a frequent guest in the country for academic conferences, was traveling to Yunnan province at the invitation of a Chinese academic institution. He was detained upon arrival at the airport on June 3. China has accused Min Zin of spying and endangering China’s national security.

Following a recent meeting with Min Zin, U.S. consular officers described increasingly hostile treatment from Chinese authorities, who employed deliberate tactics to disrupt and frustrate conversations to limit the time in which American officials could talk about substantive issues, according to an account of the visit.

Chinese authorities barred U.S. officials from discussing with Min Zin any questions related to his case, interrogation, treatment, work on Myanmar or colleagues. Officials would receive a warning if they violated any of these terms, and a second violation would end the visit immediately.

A consular officer, who has dealt with Americans detained in China for more than two years, called it one of the most disruptive and restrictive visits he’s ever experienced, according to the account.

U.S. officials are also concerned about Chinese authorities restricting humanitarian requests for Min Zin, including blocking reading materials, refusing to provide outside allergy medication — saying that the authorities would provide their own — and a new account from him of knee pain, raising concern of ill treatment. A person familiar with Min Zin said he never had knee pain before. There’s also concern that he is living with constant light, blocking his ability to sleep.

Despite this, officials described Min Zin as mentally resilient and physically stable, maintaining a meditation practice and eating meals provided by authorities, and they said he was preparing himself for an extended imprisonment, requiring endurance and resilience. The interruptions and delay tactics employed by Chinese authorities limited the 30-minute conversation to about 15 minutes, the account estimated, but Min Zin used the time to relay to his family that they prioritize their health and exercise vigilance at home, based on worries about transnational Chinese repression.

The Hill has reached out to the State Department and Chinese Embassy in Washington, D.C., for comment.

Min Zin is a native of Myanmar and participated as a student in the country’s 1988 democracy movement. He studied political science at the University of California, Berkeley and later established in Myanmar an independent think tank, the Institute for Strategy and Policy. He left the country after the military coup in 2021. China is Myanmar’s most powerful and influential neighbor.

Sylvia Zin said her husband traveled to China “in pursuit of academic exchange and because he deeply values the people to people ties that can be built over the sharing of ideas.”

“Min Zin believed that the PRC understood the importance of academic cooperation, but the arrest of an American academic sends the opposite message,” she said.

A U.S. official told Reuters that Min Zin’s detention “has raised grave concerns among other scholars about ​whether they could be ⁠subject to entrapment and detention by China,” hitting on a pressure point for Beijing as they look to increase people-to-people ties and academic exchange with the U.S.

“The safety and security of U.S. citizens globally is President Trump’s top priority, and the president has been clear that China must treat U.S. citizens with respect — and those wrongfully detained or under exit bans must be released,” the official said.

Min Zin is the second American considered “wrongfully detained,” following the arrest in 2024 of Youlin Chen, a Chinese-born American seismologist. He was designated in March, and his case was made public in July. House lawmakers have cited human rights groups saying an estimated 200 Americans are detained in China, including under exit bans that prevent them from leaving the country.

Trump raised Chen’s case with Xi when the two met in Beijing in May , and the Chinese leader committed to look into it, according to a source familiar with the matter, but the family has received no indication that Chen’s case is being considered.

But in an extraordinary move last month, China released Ezra Jin, a Chinese Christian pastor whose daughter is American, after Trump raised his detention with Xi.

articles.title: David Jolly: ‘I don’t care about the left-right spectrum’
articles.summary: Florida’s Democratic nominee for governor, David Jolly, said Wednesday he’s not focused on the political divide within the party but rather is seeking solutions to big-ticket issues impacting voters ahead of the midterm elections. “I’m in a very postpartisan, postideological space. I reject the left-right spectrum. I don’t care about the left-right spectrum. We have…
articles.body:
Florida’s Democratic nominee for governor, David Jolly, said Wednesday he’s not focused on the political divide within the party but rather is seeking solutions to big-ticket issues impacting voters ahead of the midterm elections.

“I’m in a very postpartisan, postideological space. I reject the left-right spectrum. I don’t care about the left-right spectrum. We have big problems that need big solutions. So what I did as a Democrat is amplify the fundamental values in our party, that the economy should work for everybody,” Jolly said during a Wednesday appearance on NewsNation’s “Cuomo.”

“Economic growth is good, but it’s got to work for everybody. The private sector should lead, but government needs to fill in the gaps,” he added.

Jolly served in the House as a Republican before becoming an independent in 2019 following woes with President Trump.

Last year, he registered as a Democrat and launched his gubernatorial bid within a new party.

His campaign has coincided with a growing progressive pulse within the faction focused on improving healthcare, housing, safety and the environment, which Jolly has said are of concern to all people.

The Democratic gubernatorial nominee firmly stated he was a capitalist in favor of the private economy and rejected ties to socialism during the “Cuomo” segment.

However, he said democratic socialists including Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon (D) are gaining momentum by outlining a plan to address the economic crisis impacting Americans nationwide.

“Our politics are very different. We disagree on a whole lot,” Jolly said of Nixon and democratic socialists.

“But the reality is, I think in each one of these races, to your point, Democratic candidates were addressing the economic crisis that is real. That is real,” he added.

Jolly continued to state that Republicans’ “major fault” is refusing to recognize the economic anxiety.

“They’re following the Trump playbook of just telling people that what they’re feeling is wrong. Republicans are out of touch. Democrats have an opportunity this year,” he added.

Jolly will face off against Trump endorsed Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) in November, while Nixon is challenging Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.) for her seat in the upper chamber.

articles.title: Meet the men applying for the 'hardest job in British politics'
articles.summary: Labour MSPs Michael Marra and Joe Fagan are making their pitches as they aim to succeed Anas Sarwar.
articles.body:
Wanted: one leader for Scottish Labour. Must enjoy long hours, complex trade-offs and difficult questions.

That may not be the official job description for Scottish Labour leader, but it's perhaps not far from the truth.

After all, Anas Sarwar described this gig as "the hardest job in British politics".

Despite this health warning, two candidates are on the ballot paper vying to take on the challenge - Michael Marra and Joe Fagan.

I sat down with both of them for the Scotcast podcast to learn a bit about who they are, where they think Labour has gone wrong, and their prescription for fixing things.

Scottish Labour leader hopefuls warn against party divisions Published 12 August

Scottish Labour leader hopefuls warn against party divisions

Lennon criticises 'nasty' Scottish Labour as leadership bid fails Published 17 August

Lennon criticises 'nasty' Scottish Labour as leadership bid fails

But before we got into the nitty gritty of politics, I wanted to know a bit more about these two candidates.

We started with an ice-breaker: If they had to give a Ted Talk (an online lecture about a topic they're passionate about), what would their subject be?

For Michael Marra, it was his beloved football team, Dundee United.

Given they've just endured back-to-back 4-0 defeats, there's a joke here about the North East Labour MSP backing lost causes.

Joe Fagan opted for a lecture on Cold War Berlin.

And there was even a comparison about the "eerie resemblance" between Stasi HQ in East Germany and the office he occupied when he was the leader of South Lanarkshire Council.

But we weren't here to talk about DUFC's glory days or the fall of the wall. This was a conversation about everything that's been going on with Scottish Labour.

The most newsworthy reflection probably came from Fagan, the South of Scotland MSP, who was critical of Sarwar's decision to leave Holyrood and take a place in the House of Lords.

He wished Sarwar well on a personal level, but said it "wasn't a good look" for him to stop being a Glasgow MSP and head to Westminster's upper chamber.

Fagan said that he would never personally take a seat in the Lords. And not just because he thinks the robes look "ridiculous".

But he did concede that it would be difficult to turn down the offer of a ministerial post from the prime minister.

Michael Marra also had some criticisms of Anas Sarwar's approach as leader.

He praised his work ethic and communication abilities, but said that the party had been too focused on Sarwar in the last five years.

Privately other party figures have said that same â that the party's style was too "presidential" in recent years, rather than showcasing a team of spokespeople.

Marra told me the party had "lost definition as to who the Labour Party is" and had become "too narrow in our leadership and the circle of influence around the leader".

A big question hanging over these interviews was what will the approach of these candidates be to independence?

While Scottish Labour isn't going to support that sort of constitutional change any time soon (or perhaps ever), there are voices inside the party who argue it's time to engage with the debate around the grounds for a second referendum.

But both Michael Marra and Joe Fagan don't have much time for this argument.

Fagan said it would be "obvious" when the will of the Scottish people had changed, but we weren't at that point.

He insisted that debates around the process for independence was a relic of the "Sturgeon era", and that that period was now "history".

Marra told me he wasn't clear how a trigger for a second referendum would work, arguing that people are more concerned with issues like the cost of living and the NHS.

This leadership contest has â somewhat unexpectedly â focussed on the issue of gender in recent days.

When Glasgow MSP Monica Lennon failed to make the ballot , she released an explosive statement suggesting the other two had been "punching down on trans people".

Both Marra and Fagan have rejected that accusation. But they both have strong views on the issue of gender reform.

Remember, MSPs passed a bill in 2022 that would have made it easier for someone to change their legally recognised sex â so-called "self-ID".

It was ultimately blocked by the UK government, a decision upheld in the courts.

Labour MSPs at the time were whipped to support it. Some gave up their spokesperson positions in order to vote against.

Marra came to a deal with Sarwar â he was allowed to abstain.

But he told Scotcast he felt so strongly about the issue that he would've been willing to resign over it.

Fagan wasn't in Holyrood at the time, but his view watching from outside was that Labour MSPs shouldn't have backed it.

When it came to the economic side of Scottish politics, both candidates expressed the view that some Scots â especially middle earners â are paying too much tax.

But that doesn't necessarily mean cuts across the board.

Fagan argued that there's a case for "widening" the tax base through some new approaches, such as environmental taxes.

And Marra â whose professional background is in economics â said that he was willing to consider looking at a wealth tax.

And when it comes to oil and gas both wannabee leaders think the UK government should go ahead with extracting at the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields.

Scotcast - The Scottish Labour leadership interviews

Michael Marra and Joe Fagan are vying to succeed Anas Sarwar as Scottish Labour leader. They talk to us about their partyâs failures, the route to indyref2 and guilty pleasures.

Some in Labour were unhappy when Lennon didn't make the ballot for this contesting, lamenting a lack of breadth in the contest.

And they maybe have a point. It doesn't feel like Scottish Labour members are choosing between two radically different candidates here. This pair broadly agree on a lot.

That being said, both Marra and Fagan seem thoughtful, eloquent and capable politicians.

But the trajectory of Scottish Labour's Holyrood results make for grim reading â they've lost MSPs at every election since 1999.

A once mighty political force in Scotland has just 17 MSPs now.

It's a movement that requires a massive shot of adrenaline. It needs something that can win back its once natural voters, who seem to have found political homes elsewhere.

It doesn't feel like either Fagan or Marra have outlined that recovery plan yet. And, to be fair, they have a bit of time until they face the public again.

But they will need to outline that grand idea at some point. Or the winner risks simply being the latest captain of a political ship that's sinking in the rough seas of Scottish politics.

articles.title: Hutchinson on NRSC data centers memo: ‘Alarmist’ tone ‘concerning’
articles.summary: Former Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson (R) called a recent private memo from the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) about data centers “alarmist in tone.” Appearing on NewsNation, Hutchinson told host Blake Burman, “The NRSC memo was almost alarmist in tone, which is concerning in and of itself.” “Republican candidates need to define themselves on the…
articles.body:
Former Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson (R) called a recent private memo from the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) about data centers “alarmist in tone.”

Appearing on NewsNation, Hutchinson told host Blake Burman, “The NRSC memo was almost alarmist in tone, which is concerning in and of itself.”

“Republican candidates need to define themselves on the issue of data centers and their expansions and building them in our communities before they are defined on it and before it becomes a bigger issue,” Hutchinson continued.

The NRSC memo, titled “ Ohio Data Center Risk ,” was sent to AI companies, arguing if incumbent Ohio Sen. Jon Husted (R) loses his Senate election against former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) — who the memo says has made opposition to data centers the “centerpiece of his campaign against Husted” — the campaign against data centers “will expand far beyond Ohio.”

The NRSC wrote that these companies should make a better case for themselves and do it fast: explaining who benefits, who pays for higher costs and why communities should want data centers.

Some polling shows that data centers are broadly unpopular with a majority of Americans: 41 percent surveyed by Public First in July said they would oppose a data center being built near them.

Burman asked Hutchinson if he believed this movement against data centers would cause Republicans to align with Democrats as the 2026 midterms approach.

“I think they’ll be very careful in what they say. They will support data centers as long as there is local control, as long as the residential consumers don’t pay for the electricity, they pay their own way,” he said.

Hutchinson cited widespread concern from Americans on the water and energy consumption of data centers as to why data centers may be unpopular in Ohio.

Hutchinson acknowledged that data centers had been seen as “an attractive opportunity for governors to compete and to bring these data centers in,” but “now it becomes a controversial issue that you better be able to articulate clearly that you don’t want consumers to be paying for it and harmed.”

Hutchinson also mentioned President Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge, which more than 300 companies have signed on to since it was announced in March. It requires companies involved in building data center infrastructure to cover the entire energy costs .

EdgeCore Digital Infrastructure, a data center developer operating in California and Virginia, became the latest company to sign the pledge on Aug. 13 .

articles.title: To outcompete China, unhandcuff America’s biotech innovators
articles.summary: Former official David Mansdoerfer argues that bureaucratic delays at the FDA threaten American leadership in the growing regenerative medicine sector and give international competitors like China a strategic advantage.
articles.body:
America’s long-held dominance in biotechnology is slowly slipping away . China now conducts more clinical drug trials than the U.S. , and its share of global drug-development activity has grown dramatically over the past decade.

This is a problem that goes well beyond the biotech industry. The countries that can discover, develop, manufacture and commercialize the next generation of medical breakthroughs will have an enormous advantage in economic competitiveness, national security and public health.

But America still has opportunities to outcompete China, and regenerative medicine could be one of them. Regenerative treatments involve biotechnologies such as engineered tissues, biomaterials, and gene editing that seek to repair or replace damaged cells, tissues and organs. While China is active in the field , the market for this technology in the U.S. is expected to balloon to $90 billion by 2030.

The U.S. can outpace the rest of the world in this next frontier of healthcare, but only with a policy environment that encourages innovation and enables American companies to compete on equal footing with their global counterparts. That requires a nimble and dynamic regulatory process — one that makes timely decisions and gives innovators the certainty they need to create products that meet patient needs.

The consequences of delayed regulatory decisions are not hypothetical. One Florida biotechnology company has spent years living them.

Based in Pensacola, Regenative Labs develops products for patients derived from donated human birth tissue. Although patients and physicians across the U.S. have benefited from Regenative’s cutting-edge biotech, the company can’t serve patients overseas. That’s because the FDA won’t make a decision on the company’s applications for a Certificate of Foreign Government, a document needed to sell to foreign markets. For three years, dating back to the Biden administration, the company has been mired in bureaucratic delay , waiting endlessly for a decision that federal law requires the FDA to make within 20 days.

While bureaucrats have dithered, foreign competitors unbound by the FDA’s rules have gained a leg up and a chunk of market share abroad. The easy solution for Regenative would be to pack up and move its operations offshore, but it wants to stay and grow in Florida, where it began. An American company with American-developed technology has been put at a competitive disadvantage and held back from expanding its workforce, not because of a lack of demand for its products, but because bureaucrats have ignored their congressional mandate to act.

This case is about more than one company’s export applications. It demonstrates how regulatory inaction can limit biotech growth, slow manufacturing, and weaken America’s position in one of the world’s fastest-growing industries. Every delayed decision is a missed opportunity for American workers, domestic manufacturing, and the homegrown companies developing the next generation of medical innovation.

The situation reflects a broader reality. Biotechnology is rapidly becoming one of the defining industries of the 21st century. The countries that discover, develop and produce tomorrow’s medical breakthroughs will shape the future and come out on top. Maintaining American leadership in biotech means ensuring that pipeline journey happens here at home.

The U.S. has long been the world’s standard bearer in medical innovation, but that status is in jeopardy. China has its sights on overtaking us as the global leader in biotech. We cannot take our leadership in this arena for granted. Every time unnecessary bureaucracy hamstrings American innovators while competitors abroad move ahead, we risk surrendering a strategic advantage that has taken half a century to build.

The benefits of American biotechnology extend far beyond commercial markets and America’s borders. American-developed medical innovations have the potential to improve care for hundreds of thousands of U.S. service members, military families and other Americans living overseas. Why would we prevent America’s service men and women and their families abroad from accessing new treatments that could improve their health?

Making America Healthy Again isn’t just about discovering new ways to be healthy. It’s about creating conditions that allow innovation to reach patients. Our regulatory system must provide the clarity American companies need to succeed. Transparency and timely action from our agencies are as important as anything else to advancing better health and preserving U.S. leadership in biotechnology for years to come.

David Mansdoerfer is the former Deputy Assistant Secretary for Health and currently serves as an adjunct professor in health policy and politics at Pepperdine University School of Public Policy.

articles.title: Lindell says he’d spend ‘upwards of $1 million’ in private Minnesota primary recount
articles.summary: MyPillow founder Mike Lindell said Wednesday he’s prepared to spend “upwards of $1 million” for a private recount of ballots cast in the Minnesota Republican primary for governor. Minnesota state House Speaker Lisa Demuth (R) beat Lindell by 11 percentage points, but Lindell has refused to cede to the lawmaker, citing concerns with voting machines…
articles.body:
MyPillow founder Mike Lindell said Wednesday he’s prepared to spend “upwards of $1 million” for a private recount of ballots cast in the Minnesota Republican primary for governor.

Minnesota state House Speaker Lisa Demuth (R) beat Lindell by 11 percentage points, but Lindell has refused to cede to the lawmaker, citing concerns with voting machines and election integrity.

“Even if this recount and audit does not overturn my election for governor of Minnesota, I believe this is the gateway to getting rid of these electronic voting machines,” Lindell wrote in a Tuesday press release .

The MyPillow founder has railed against voting machines since President Trump lost the 2020 election.

Lindell pushed to overturn the election six years ago and is now offering to pay for a full hand recount and audit of this year’s Republican primary for Minnesota’s governorship.

Costs are projected to reach $825,000, as outlined by the Minnesota secretary of State.

But Lindell says he’s prepared to spend more to hire a team of workers to oversee the state’s recount.

He faces a Monday deadline to turn in “a bond, cash or surety,” as reported by NBC News .

Lindell told the outlet he plans to “personally go in there” himself to deliver the official request Monday.

Lindell owes electronic voting system Smartmatic $56,369 in sanctions as the result of a ruling in a defamation lawsuit brought against the executive for casting doubt on the company’s election technology.

Because he refused to pay, he was held in civil contempt, racking up an additional $500 daily fine, which his lawyers say he can’t afford.

On Wednesday, Lindell’s attorneys sent a letter to U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Bryan to file a motion to reconsider the ruling holding him liable for defamation.

articles.title: El-Sayed holds slight lead over Rogers in new AARP poll
articles.summary: Progressive Abdul El-Sayed narrowly leads former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) in the race to succeed retiring Michigan Sen. Gary Peters (D), according to a new poll. An AARP poll released Thursday, which was commissioned by pollsters Fabrizio Ward and Impact Research, found El-Sayed led Rogers 48 percent to 47 percent among likely voters, with 5…
articles.body:
Progressive Abdul El-Sayed narrowly leads former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) in the race to succeed retiring Michigan Sen. Gary Peters (D), according to a new poll.

An AARP poll released Thursday , which was commissioned by pollsters Fabrizio Ward and Impact Research, found El-Sayed led Rogers 48 percent to 47 percent among likely voters, with 5 percent undecided.

The survey had a margin of error of 3.3 percentage points, making the two candidates effectively tied.

The polling showed Rogers had a higher amount of enthusiasm within his party — 96 percent — compared with the 91 percent of Democrats who support the former Wayne County health director. Notably, El-Sayed held a 6-point lead over Rogers among independents.

El-Sayed performed better with voters aged 18 to 49 years by 14 points, women by 12 points and Black voters by 41 points. Meanwhile, Rogers outperformed his opponent among voters older than 50 years by 9 points, voters older than 65 years by 13 points, men by 12 points and men older than 50 years by 21 points.

Rogers also held a 5-point advantage over El-Sayed among white voters.

El-Sayed and Rogers are duking it out for the battleground Senate seat, which Republicans view as one of their best pickup opportunities this fall.

Republicans viewed El-Sayed as the weaker Democrat in the primary against moderate Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) given his progressive stances on taxing billionaires and corporations, health care and the war in Gaza.

At the same time, Rogers has already lost a Michigan Senate race. In 2024, now-Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) defeated him. Republicans must also navigate a fraught midterm landscape and Trump’s underwater approval ratings.

A polling average of Michigan Senate general election surveys compiled by Decision Desk HQ shows El-Sayed narrowly leading Rogers 44 percent to 42 percent.

The AARP poll was conducted Aug. 9-11 with 877 likely voters surveyed statewide.

articles.title: Reverse Megxit: Prince Harry, Meghan returning to UK with their children
articles.summary: Prince Harry and his wife, Meghan, are reportedly moving back to Britain this month with their two children six years after their dramatic split from royal life and retreat to California. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex will live at a private residence outside of London while keeping their home in Montecito, Calif., and vacation…
articles.body:
Prince Harry and his wife, Meghan, are reportedly moving back to Britain this month with their two children six years after their dramatic split from royal life and retreat to California.

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex will live at a private residence outside of London while keeping their home in Montecito, Calif., and vacation property in Portugal, according to reports.

Their children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, have enrolled in British schools and will begin classes in September.

The move is a major reversal for the couple since “Megxit,” when they left Britain in 2020 after stepping back from their official royal duties amid a bitter dispute with the royal family and intense scrutiny and litigation involving the British press.

Harry and Meghan will not be returning to their royal duties once they return to England. They will remain nonworking members of the royal family and will not live at a royal residence, preserving an arrangement reached with the late Queen Elizabeth II after their initial departure.

King Charles III reportedly learned of the couple’s plans to return Sunday and welcomed the prospect of having his son and grandchildren closer. Charles had last seen Harry and Meghan’s children this summer for the first time in four years during a visit to England at his Highgrove estate.

Harry has increasingly signaled that he wants to repair his relationship with his family, particularly his father, who is being treated for an undisclosed form of cancer.

“I would love reconciliation with my family. There’s no point in continuing to fight anymore,” Harry said in an interview with the BBC last year.

Harry and Meghan’s relationship with the royal family deteriorated after the couple publicly aired their issues with several senior royals, including his older brother, Prince William and his wife, Princess Catherine, who also battled cancer.

The issues generated further headlines during an explosive interview with Oprah Winfrey in 2021, when Meghan accused an unnamed member of the royal family of inquiring about the skin color of their unborn child and accusing Catherine of making her cry. Harry also further criticized Charles’s wife, Queen Camilla, over her affair with his father while he was married to Harry’s mother, the late Princess Diana.

Harry and his family lost his taxpayer-funded police protection after stepping back from royal duties and repeatedly challenged that decision in court. He argued that the lack of security made it impossible to bring Meghan and their children to Britain safely.

Harry and Meghan, who married in 2018, have built careers outside the monarchy since moving to the U.S., including through media and business ventures. Meghan was an actress before her marriage to Harry, notably starring in the popular show “Suits.”

articles.title: Democrats press Warsh to release reported conversations with Trump
articles.summary: A group of Democrats called for Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh to publicly disclose his communications with President Trump, citing recent reporting they said raises “sincere doubts” about the central bank’s independence from the White House under his leadership. Warsh and Trump have spoken “repeatedly” since he was confirmed in April to replace former Chair…
articles.body:
A group of Democrats called for Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh to publicly disclose his communications with President Trump, citing recent reporting they said raises “sincere doubts” about the central bank’s independence from the White House under his leadership.

Warsh and Trump have spoken “repeatedly” since he was confirmed in April to replace former Chair Jerome Powell, according to The Wall Street Journal . The president has already pressured the Fed chief to consult him on interest rate decisions .

“It is critical that the Fed be transparent about these discussions to demonstrate its independence from the White House, a norm that you have said you intend to uphold,” the lawmakers wrote in the Wednesday letter .

“Instead, you have declined on multiple occasions to confirm your conversations with President Trump, raising sincere doubts about the independent conduct of monetary policy and your transparency with the public,” the group added.

Warsh stressed to lawmakers that the Fed would “remain independent on my watch” during three hours of testimony before the House Financial Services Committee last month.

“Fed independence is essential to the proper conduct of monetary policy, and I expect and will ensure that monetary policy is independent over the four years of my term,” he told Rep. Mike Flood (R-Neb.) during the hearing. “And like you, I think it provides extraordinary benefits in everything we do and strengthens the role of the United States and the U.S. dollar and the global economy.”

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) led the request, which was joined by Democratic Sens. Jack Reed (R.I.), Angela Alsobrooks (Md.) and Elizabeth Warren (Mass.).

All four lawmakers sit on the Senate Banking Committee, which has oversight authority over the central bank.

The senators said Warsh’s failure to disclose reported calls with the president is “even more curious” given that the chair’s public calendars list meetings with other senior White House officials.

“Effective conduct of monetary policy depends on transparency, accountability, and integrity from the Chair, all of which are undermined by secret conversations with the President,” the senators wrote.

“While periodic communications with the President and Administration about the state of the economy are not objectionable in and of themselves, the repeated, free-flowing conversations described in the reporting are unprecedented in the modern era,” they continued. “If true they raise serious questions about the Fed’s relationship with the White House.”

A Fed spokesperson confirmed to The Hill that the Fed’s practice of publicly listing all scheduled meetings and events has not changed and that the chair’s schedules are released with a one-month delay.

articles.title: Newsom on whether he’d be a good president: ‘I have no idea’
articles.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) said Thursday that he was unsure whether he would make a good president, amid growing speculation he will run for the White House in 2028. Asked during an interview with “Detroit Talk City” if he would be a good president, Newsom responded: “That’s a, that’s a difficult question to answer.”…
articles.body:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) said Thursday that he was unsure whether he would make a good president, amid growing speculation he will run for the White House in 2028.

Asked during an interview with “Detroit Talk City” if he would be a good president, Newsom responded: “That’s a, that’s a difficult question to answer.”

“I have no idea. I would like to think I would be, but that’s for others to determine,” he continued.

“I think I was a pretty good mayor. I think I was pretty good, but people have different opinions, and so I’m not naive about it,” he concluded.

Newsom was the mayor of San Francisco from 2004 to 2011 before becoming California’s governor.

The Public Policy Institute of California found in May that 50 percent of California adults approve of Newsom’s job performance as governor. This is down from October and December 2025, when Newsom’s approval rating hovered around 54 percent.

Newsom is one of several Democrats seemingly eyeing 2028 bids. Other potential candidates include Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), former Vice President Kamala Harris, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and former Rep. Rahm Emanuel (D-Ill.).

Newsom said in October 2025 that he would be “lying” if he said he wasn’t considering a bid for the White House after the 2026 midterms.

A Emerson College and The Hill survey that ranked potential match-ups between potential GOP and Democratic presidential candidates found Newsom in a decent position.

Newsom held small leads over both potential Republican nominees, Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, unlike Ocasio-Cortez, who trailed both candidates.

The survey had a margin of error of 3 percentage points.

Prediction markets still have Newsom as one of the top candidates, with Ocasio-Cortez moving ahead of him by 1 point in early prediction market odds for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination.

articles.title: Texas, Iowa Senate races shift to toss-ups: Cook Political Report
articles.summary: The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report shifted its ratings for both the Texas and Iowa Senate races to toss-ups Thursday as Republicans grapple with a scandal-ridden candidate in the Lone Star State and a shifting political environment that could favor Democrats in Iowa. Jessica Taylor, Cook Political Report Senate and governors editor, wrote…
articles.body:
The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report shifted its ratings for both the Texas and Iowa Senate races to toss-ups Thursday as Republicans grapple with a scandal-ridden candidate in the Lone Star State and a shifting political environment that could favor Democrats in Iowa.

Jessica Taylor, Cook Political Report Senate and governors editor, wrote in an analysis that polling has shown Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico with still net-positive approval ratings, while surveys have shown Texas GOP candidate Ken Paxton with high disapproval ratings and “notably underperforming even a generic Republican in GOP polling.”

Taylor noted that in addition to Paxton’s negatives, there’s also an open question of which Republican groups will invest in the Texas Senate race as Senate Republicans spent a hefty amount of money to support Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas).

Additionally, the Cook Political Report editor added that having a libertarian on the ballot could help Talarico. Some Republicans may ultimately be unwilling to vote for the Texas attorney general but may also be repelled by the idea of casting a ballot for the Democratic state lawmaker, giving them the option to vote for a third candidate, which would inevitably help Democrats.

“It’s important to note that Talarico also has liabilities that Republicans can — and will — exploit, including his comments that ‘God is non-binary’ and that there are multiple genders,” Taylor wrote.

“He’ll soon be hit with millions in ads designed to paint him as outside of the mainstream,” she continued. “But the soft-spoken seminary student also has attributes that make him appealing to disaffected Republicans, whom his campaign is aggressively targeting.”

In the Iowa Senate race, Taylor explained that the nonpartisan election handicapper was not moving the race away from Republicans because of candidate quality, noting that Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) is a strong recruit and fundraiser.

But she noted that shifting political winds are offering state Rep. Josh Turek (D) a potential opening in a state that voted for President Trump by 13 points in 2024.

“Three of the four congressional seats are competitive, and the open governor’s race is moving away from them,” Taylor wrote.

“Rising fertilizer and diesel prices, in addition to tariffs, have uniquely harmed the state’s agriculture-dependent economy,” she added.

And like Texas, Taylor said the presence of a libertarian on the ballot could similarly help Turek, though she noted that Democrats still have an uphill climb ahead.

“Turek needs to raise more money if this is going to remain a top-tier opportunity for Democrats, but the early spending Republicans are already deploying to define Turek shows they’re concerned about their prospects in this now-battleground state,” she wrote.

Taylor made a caveat that the race ratings for both elections could change, as campaigns haven’t started seriously spending yet and that current polling could show more of a “sugar high” for Democrats in this midterm environment.

The Cook Political Report editor also noted that Republicans have a clear financial advantage over Democrats — turbocharged further by a recent Supreme Court ruling that has allowed parties and campaigns to coordinate, fundraise and spend unlimited amounts of money.

“Republicans have an unmistakable financial advantage that could revitalize their sagging candidates, but it may not be able to make up for the sizable voter enthusiasm gap that Democrats have on their side,” Taylor wrote.
